title: Why the mean minimizes squared error

source.title: Original worked example: least-squares constant theorem

cues.title: Which constant best represents these numbers?

sentences.say: Suppose we want to replace several real numbers by one constant, while minimizing their average squared error.
We will prove that the unique best constant is their arithmetic mean.

cues.note: A worked example: 1, 3, 5. Their arithmetic mean is 3.

cues.title: Define the average and the objective

sentences.say: There are n real numbers, with n at least one. Their arithmetic mean is x bar.
For any proposed constant a, F of a is the average squared distance from those numbers.

cues.title: Deviations from the mean add to zero

sentences.say: The crucial observation is that the signed deviations from the mean add to zero.
This follows directly from the definition of the arithmetic mean.

cues.title: Separate the data deviation and the constant shift

sentences.say: Write each error as the deviation from the mean plus the shift from a to the mean.
Squaring gives three terms: a squared deviation, a cross term, and a squared shift.

cues.title: The cross term cancels after summing

sentences.say: The shift is the same for every data point, so it can come outside the sum.
What remains is the sum of deviations, which we already showed is zero.

cues.title: An exact identity, valid for every constant

sentences.say: The average of n identical squared shifts is just one squared shift.
We obtain this exact identity, with no approximation and no omitted terms.

cues.note: Every real value of a is covered by the calculation.

cues.title: A square is nonnegative, and vanishes only at zero

sentences.say: The extra square is nonnegative, so no constant can beat the mean.
Equality holds only when a equals the mean. That proves both global optimality and uniqueness.

cues.title: See the minimum in a concrete example

sentences.say: For the values one, three, and five, the mean is three and the minimum average loss is eight thirds.
The curve rises by exactly the square of the distance from three. The numerical picture illustrates the proof.

cues.note: Illustration for (1,3,5); the preceding algebra proves the general case.
